blindSummary:
This is a historically progressive destination where trans visitors face little risk. It was the first country in its region to introduce legal gender recognition by self-declaration (2014), has banned conversion therapy (2023), offers nonbinary gender markers, and has comprehensive anti-discrimination protections covering gender identity. There is no rollback movement, and the capital ranks among the world's most LGBTQ+-welcoming cities.

One documented weakness: the supreme court ruled in 2024 that a trans woman who legally changed her gender but hasn't had surgery must serve in a men's prison and be strip-searched by male staff — finding this did not violate the regional human-rights convention. This is the same prison-placement issue documented in several other destination countries. The national human-rights institute also flags that police under-investigate hate crimes and are not obliged to flag hate-crime motivation at the time of reporting.

Anti-trans discourse is intensifying (a debate over lowering the age limit for legal gender recognition; an opinion piece by a former equality minister presenting trans people as a threat to gender equality) but has not produced rollback legislation.
blindOutOfScope: No trans-specific travel advisory; general urban crime is low.
blindSourceSummaries: Independent newsroom (Sept 2024): this country marks 10 years as the first in its region with legal self-ID gender recognition (2014); the debate has stayed cool - no criminal incidents recorded since the law passed, and even a contested prison-placement ruling failed to ignite a political storm. It was also the first in the world to recognise same-sex partnerships (1989).

International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): robust protections - marriage and adoption, SOGISC discrimination prohibited, self-determined legal gender markers, nonbinary 'X' passports, blood-donation rules based on practices not identity (July 2024), comprehensive LGBTIQ-inclusive sex education; 93% public support for same-sex relationships (2023 regional survey).

Commercial broadcaster (Sept 2024): the country's supreme court ruled that a trans prisoner (legally changed gender in 2015, no surgery) must serve her sentence in a men's unit - the case passed without major political controversy.
The national human-rights institute's LGBT barometer page on discrimination and hatred - monitoring of discrimination and hate incidents against LGBT people in this country.

Regional LGBTI-rights organisation's annual review 2024 (covering 2023), chapter on this country: anti-trans and anti-gender discourse intensified during the parliamentary debate on lowering the age limit for legal gender recognition (religious websites accused trans groups of taking children 'hostage'); the UN anti-torture committee flagged nonconsensual intersex surgeries; trans people and migrants reported being denied access to spaces and services.

Regional LGBTI-rights organisation's annual review 2025 (covering 2024), chapter on this country: a former equality minister published an opinion piece presenting trans and intersex people as a threat to gender equality (she was reassigned from her portfolio); in July a migrant trans woman was murdered in a hotel room in the capital; the anti-torture committee's concerns over nonconsensual intersex surgeries persist.

Travel-safety site page on the capital (2026): safety confidence scores (LGBTQ+ 91, trans 89, rated 'safe'); legal status summary (partnerships 1989, marriage 2012, self-declaration since 2014, conversion-therapy ban 2023); describes the capital as compact, walkable and exceptionally safe.
Global rights-perception survey's country profile for this country: composite LGBT-rights perception scores including a global transgender-rights index.

News outlet (Feb 2013): a trans woman became the first transgender person granted asylum in this country - she had feared persecution for her trans activism in her home country (police attacks and threats); initially refused by the refugee appeals board, her case was reopened after a national LGBT organisation provided documentation.
blindLocalsOnly: The self-declaration legal-gender-recognition regime (2014, nonbinary markers) is resident-facing; the 2024 supreme court prison-placement ruling and the age-limit debate concern residents.
